study.title: Deuteronomy 6 The central commandment, the memory of redemption and the formation of faith in the family
study.overview: In this chapter, Moses shows that obedience to God is not only an external duty, but a response of love, reverence and grateful memory. The text unites teaching, practice and generational transmission: Israel must keep the commandments, love the Lord whole, remember the liberation of Egypt and continually teach these truths to the children. The chapter also warns against forgetfulness, idolatry, and the attempt to put God to the test. At the end, obedience is presented as the way in which the righteousness of the people is evident before the Lord.

outline.title: The commandments should be received and practiced
outline.explanation: Moses presents the commandments, statutes, and regulations as divine instruction to be obeyed in the promised land. The purpose is to produce reverent fear, continuous fidelity and lasting well-being for the people and their generations.

outline.title: The center of faith: to love the Lord and to keep his word in his heart
outline.explanation: Israel is called to confess that the Lord is one and to love him with total completeness. These words must dwell in the heart and be repeated to the children, at home and on the way, showing that faith must shape the whole life and the family memory.

outline.title: Prosperity, forgetfulness and exclusivity of worship
outline.explanation: When the people enter the land and receive houses, cities and harvests that he has not built, they must remember that everything comes from the Lord. The text warns against forgetting the God who delivered Israel from Egypt, following other gods, testing the Lord and abandoning the commandments, for he is a zealous God who demands faithfulness.

outline.title: The catechesis of children and justice by obedience
outline.explanation: When the children ask the meaning of the laws, the answer must begin with the history of slavery in Egypt and the powerful deliverance of the Lord. The end of these commandments is the good of the people, their life, and their distinction as just before God in practicing all that he commanded.

study.context: The chapter belongs to Moses" discourse and resumes the covenant logic already presented before: God teaches, the people hear, guard and transmit. The notes highlight that Moses was preparing Israel to live in the promised land, and that instruction should continue from generation to generation. There is also reference to the later use of these words by Jesus when he was tempted, which shows his centrality in the biblical faith. It is not necessary to assume more historical details than the text itself provides: the focus is on the passage of the people of Egypt to the land sworn to the patriarchs.
study.theology: Deuteronomy 6 teaches that true biblical religion begins with the confession of the Lord's uniqueness and expresses itself in total love, reverent fear and concrete obedience. The love requested is not only emotion; it includes mind, will, affections and strengths, that is, the whole person turned to God. The memory of Egypt's redemption prevents prosperity from producing pride or idolatry. Obedience also has a pedagogical dimension: faith must be taught to children at all times of life. In verse 25, justice is presented as evidenced by obedience, not as autonomous merit; the notes interpret this as a sign of the condition of those who are already in correct relationship with God by faith and divine mercy. Thus, the practice of commandments manifests fidelity of covenant, reverence and gratitude.

scholarViews.insight: Love of the Lord involves the whole person: understanding, will, emotions and strength. This commandment is the center of the covenant and is resumed by Jesus as a summary of human obligation before God.
Moses teaches only what God has commanded, and the purpose of teaching is that the people practice. The instruction received aggravates the responsibility if it is not lived.
Obedience must be continuous and generational: whoever fears God must seek to form children in righteousness so that true religion remains in the family.

questions: How can I demonstrate, in daily practice, that I love the Lord with wholeness and not just with words?
How does the remembrance of God's deliverance correct the tendency to forget the Lord when everything goes well?
Have I taught my family to speak of faith at home, on the way, to lie down and when I lifted up, or have I treated obedience as something private and occasional?
study.practice: Set up a daily moment to read this chapter, memorize verses 4 and 5 and turn them into prayer. Then choose a concrete way to transmit faith to someone in the house: a conversation, a question, a brief explanation of what God did, or a memory of the Lord's character. It is also worth examining whether any blessing received has occupied the place of gratitude and fidelity to God Himself.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided are irregular in length and depth; therefore, some statements about the whole chapter depend more on the biblical text than on detailed comments. It is also prudent to read the statement that obedience is 'justice' in verse 25 in the light of the commentary itself, which understands it as evidence of a correct relationship with God, and not as salvation by human merit.
